newsitem.title: UK: Action man Simpson's reputation on line at GEC.
newsitem.headline: Action man Simpson's reputation on line at GEC.

text.p: George Simpson's reputation as the action man of British industry is on the line as he sets out to reshape General Electric Co Plc.
"It's like trying to wake up an elephant," says one ex-employee of the U.K. engineering group where, after 10 years of apparent stagnation, investors are clamouring for change.
Simpson, the new managing director, is a Scot who trained in accountancy and cut his teeth at car-maker Rover before selling it to Germany's BMW.
Hopes are high that his experience and contacts garnered while serving as deputy managing director at British Aerospace Plc could lead to an elusive merger with GEC.
Before joining GEC in September, Simpson's parting shot as boss of Lucas Industries was to merge it with Varity Corp of the U.S., giving LucasVarity Plc the critical mass to develop.
Simpson has wasted little time in stepping out of the shadow of his predecessor Lord Weinstock when this week he announced a shake-up designed to awaken GEC from years of strategic slumber.

But after market hopes of a signed-sealed-and-delivered European defence merger were dashed, some market participants were disappointed to see that shareholder value would be delivered over a longer time-frame than initially hoped for.

Simpson has offered a possible four billion pounds ($6.7 billion) float of the 50-50 GEC-Alsthom rail and power joint venture, making its defence unit GEC-Marconi the new heart of the group through acquisitions and holding onto and repositioning its telecoms joint venture GPT.
Industry analysts say the full impact of his gameplan is likely to be felt two to three years down the line and the jury was split on whether this was soon enough.
"GEC did not go out of its way to correct the speculation," said one analyst. "So there is disillusion. The promise of jam tomorrow -- a typical GEC story."
But others said it was unrealistic to expect mega-deals so soon, especially in the sensitive area of defence where political issues are entwined.
"The speculation jumped the gun and when nothing happened people were disappointed," said Sanjay Jha at Williams de Broe.

"My view is Simpson cannot change GEC in a day. You are not going to invest in GEC for a sharp increase in profits this year but for a return further down the line. In the long term the big deal will happen."
Simpson has held out the possibility of some short-term shareholder value through the GEC-Alsthom flotation, with a decision in three months. If the float is agreed it could happen within the year.

The one billion pounds plus cash mountain (excluding joint venture cash) which Weinstock sat on in his final years as chief will also be released and spent on acquisitions to bolster core sectors or possibly fund a share-buyback if no deals emerge.
The moves were bold by traditional GEC standards. But even with the flotation sweetener, some investors were left with the bitter taste of disappointment.
Looking ahead, it is clear that unless a major breakthrough defence deal emerges, the ability to create value in the short term is constrained.
Many of the strategic efforts remain no more than paper plans at this stage which left some investors still itchy for action and asking questions.
They wonder whether GEC can clinch a defence link-up which will catapult it into the kind of major league currently occupied by the U.S. defence industry giants after rapid consolidation.
The pressure is on following recent U.S. mega-mergers between Lockheed Martin Corp and Northrop Grumman Corp and Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas.

Analysts say GEC could afford to spend two billion pounds on defence deals and Simpson has said he is willing to gear up GEC if necessary. "The mere fact that I will now do that is a very significant change in GEC's policy," Simpson told Reuters.
He said he continued to talk to British Aerospace Plc, but added that the defence link-up talks with Italy's Finmeccanica SpA and the final bid for Siemens AG's defence arm were more immediate aims.
Analysts and press commentators had whipped up a storm of speculation before the review announcement, building hopes of a defence wedding between GEC and BAe or Finmeccanica but nothing happened.

The hoped-for asset swap with Siemens AG also failed to materialise. Analysts had speculated that GEC would trade its 60 percent stake in the telecoms joint venture GPT in return for Siemens' defence arm which is up for sale.

GEC-Marconi's most obvious defence partner is Thomson-CSF of France. But domestic political stumbling blocks have prevented the company being merged with a foreign firm. Marconi also partly matches up to the business of Alenia Difensa of Italy and Daimler-Benz Aerospace of Germany.

Williams de Broe's Jha believes the BAe deal would be best because "at least GEC would know it was merging with a company which is run efficiently and knows the meaning of value. It won't yield major cost savings but it will position it for bigger deals."

GEC-Marconi will acquire a minority stake in Finmeccanica's Alenia Difensa's avionics unit and Alenia Difensia will acquire a minority stake in GEC-Marconi's armaments and armoured vehicles business.

"This joint venture is in effect a merger of these businesses," Kemp said, adding that the combined turnover of the businesses involved was around two billion stg. "It is a very significant development and reflects a lot of work on both sides."
He said the two companies already had links through working together on a range of defence projects. No name has been decided yet for the venture. A joint management team is currently being chosen.

Kemp said the geographic fit between the two sides was good. "We are strong in different markets to the Italians. They are strong in the Middle East, Latin America and the British are strong in the Far East, the old Commonwealth countries, Canada and North America, for example."

He said the emphasis would be less focused on cost savings and more on widening the product range and sharing research and development costs. "It's a consolidation of the industry rather than rationalisation of capacity," Kemp said.
